info.bio:
The Kinks fue un grupo musical británico formado en Londres en los años 60 por los hermanos Ray y Dave Davies. Desde sus primeros tiempos estaban muy influenciados por el Rock and roll y el Rhythm & blues estadounidenses.
En 1964 consiguieron su primer Nº 1 en las listas británicas con “You Really Got Me”, su canción más emblemática, dándose a conocer como parte de la Invasión Británica en Estados Unidos (Nº 7 en Billboard) Esta canción

notes.chapter: Febrero: 19th Nervous Breakdown: la cultura adolescente británica y la locura del Swinging London
notes.text: Ray Davies, complejo y escurridizo, convertía el resentimiento en inspiración: «A Well Respected Man» retrata la hipocresía de la clase media alta con ritmo de music hall y «Where Have All the Good Times Gone» medita sobre lo ganado y lo perdido. «Dedicated Follower of Fashion» (febrero de 1966) es una canción del Swinging London hecha por londinenses sarcásticos que conocían el ejército de Carnaby Street desde dentro, con alusiones gais («frilly nylon panties»). Tras ella, Davies sufrió una crisis nerviosa en marzo: metió el televisor en el horno al verse en Top of the Pops.

notes.chapter: Agosto: Do You Come Here Often? Joe Meek, los derechos gais y un verano de violencia
notes.text: «Sunny Afternoon», escrita tras su crisis, fue la cuarta y mejor de sus canciones de comentario social: un aristócrata ocioso en su mansión, un himno veraniego con presagios de decadencia cantado con acento deliberadamente inglés. En la cara B, «I’m Not Like Everybody Else», con un Dave Davies amenazante, era pura alienación del outsider.

notes.chapter: Noviembre: Good Vibrations: Motown y el soul en Reino Unido, los Beach Boys y el Sunset Strip
notes.text: «Dead End Street» (18 de noviembre), grabada mientras llegaban las noticias de Aberfan, es una canción de la depresión moderna sobre la clase de la que Davies había escapado, gente sin salida y «estrictamente de segunda». Davies la regrabó con un trombonista sacado de un pub a espaldas de Shel Talmy y se demostró que no necesitaba productor. La BBC prohibió el vídeo, con los Kinks llevando un ataúd por Camden. En la cara B, «Big Black Smoke», una fábula hogarthiana sobre una fugada a la que Londres convierte en prostituta.

refs.q: the Kinks’ ‘Till the End of the Day’ and the Spencer Davis Group’s ‘Keep on Running’
refs.para: The UK chart was similarly burdened with seasonal sentimentality, but the Top 10 was leavened by three tough records: the Beatles’ ‘Day Tripper’, the Kinks’ ‘Till the End of the Day’ and the Spencer Davis Group’s ‘Keep on Running’ – one of the first convincing UK marriages of soul and white mod pop. By the end of the month, Otis Redding was approaching the Top 10 with his cover of the Temptations’ ‘My Girl’ and Bob Dylan’s decidedly bizarre ‘Can You Please Crawl Out Your Window?’ had entered the Top 20.
refs.chapter: Enero: A Quiet Explosion: la CND, la protesta y la conspiración del silencio

refs.q: ‘Dedicated Follower of Fashion’ is a Swinging London song by sarcastic, cynical young Londoners.
refs.para: ‘Dedicated Follower of Fashion’ is a Swinging London song by sarcastic, cynical young Londoners. The Kinks were close enough to the Carnabetian army to know whereof they spoke: ‘One week he’s in polka dots, the next week he’s in stripes.’ Bassist Pete Quaife and Dave Davies were well-known fashion plates, the latter outrageous in his shoulder-length long hair, stripy pullovers, Rupert Bear checked hipsters and – to promote the song – thigh-length rubber waders.
refs.chapter: Febrero: 19th Nervous Breakdown: la cultura adolescente británica y la locura del Swinging London

refs.q: On 17 March, Ray Davies had a major episode that involved him attacking his publicist Brian Somerville
refs.para: On 17 March, Ray Davies had a major episode that involved him attacking his publicist Brian Somerville: ‘It was like Morgan: A Suitable Case for Treatment when I look back on it, but at the time it was deadly serious.’ As ‘Dedicated Follower of Fashion’ rose in the charts, he was tormented by people coming up to him in the street and repeating his words: ‘Oh yes he is, oh yes he is.’ When he saw himself performing the song on Top of the Pops, he put the TV set in the oven and then went to bed for a week.
refs.chapter: Febrero: 19th Nervous Breakdown: la cultura adolescente británica y la locura del Swinging London

refs.q: This was the fourth and the greatest in the Kinks’ contemporary run of social commentary songs
refs.para: This was the fourth and the greatest in the Kinks’ contemporary run of social commentary songs, preceded by ‘A Well Respected Man’, ‘Where Have All the Good Times Gone?’ and ‘Dedicated Follower of Fashion’. It wasn’t a raver but a mid-paced, almost music-hall piece, as the Kinks developed the descending riff into a devastating portrait of an upper-class waster in his stately home – a summer anthem with dark presentiments of decay.
refs.chapter: Agosto: Do You Come Here Often? Joe Meek, los derechos gais y un verano de violencia

refs.q: ‘I wanted to write a modern-day depression song,’ he told me
refs.para: Over the previous year, from autumn 1965 onwards, Davies had satirised the bourgeoisie, the mods of Swinging London and the upper classes. In autumn 1966, he turned his attention to the class that had spawned him and from which, thanks to his talent, luck and drive, he had escaped. ‘I wanted to write a modern-day depression song,’ he told me, ‘because I felt that’s what was happening around me. It’s about people who’ve got no way out, saying, “What’s gone wrong? We were promised the good life – what are we living for?”’
refs.chapter: Noviembre: Good Vibrations: Motown y el soul en Reino Unido, los Beach Boys y el Sunset Strip

refs.q: ‘Dead End Street’ didn’t sound like anything else in the charts
refs.para: ‘Dead End Street’ didn’t sound like anything else in the charts, whether ballads, Tamla and soul, beat, commercial pop or the early shoots of psychedelia. Shortly afterwards, the BBC banned the ‘sick’ promo film. ‘There’s nothing funny about old people dying,’ Top of the Pops producer Stanley Dorfman told Disc and Music Echo, ‘and the Kinks couldn’t make up their minds whether to be funny or serious. The still shots showed dead and poor people and I didn’t like it.’ Ray Davies had delivered, in a sense, a dose of unwelcome reality.
refs.chapter: Noviembre: Good Vibrations: Motown y el soul en Reino Unido, los Beach Boys y el Sunset Strip

scenes.name: 1966: el año del single
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: El libro son doce ensayos, uno por mes, cada uno a partir de un single. 1966 fue el último año en que el 45 fue la forma principal del pop, antes de que Sgt. Pepper’s convirtiera el LP en la fuerza creativa y comercial en el verano de 1967: en dos o tres minutos cabían ideas, actitudes, letras y experimentos que después se estirarían en álbumes de cuarenta minutos. El pop dejó de ser comercio, romance adolescente o diversión para volverse una experiencia total, «la única cosa viva» según Lou Reed, y el prisma con el que se interpretaba el mundo. El año empezó en el pop y acabó en el rock; empezó en la Gran Sociedad de Johnson y acabó con el resurgir republicano. Hubo ambición, aceleración y compresión, y una reacción proporcional de quienes veían que todo cambiaba demasiado deprisa. Savage, que cumplió trece años ese verano escuchando Radio Caroline South, se ciñe a los singles, sobre todo los que entraron en las listas de Billboard y Record Retailer, y deja fuera el free jazz, el minimalismo, el ska, los happenings y los situacionistas.

scenes.name: Protometal: volumen, distorsión y moteros
scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: Los precursores que aportan piezas sueltas del código: el volumen como estética (Blue Cheer, MC5), el sonido de guitarra grueso y distorsionado (los Kinks en «You Really Got Me»), la contundencia de los Who en directo (Townshend presume de que Live at Leeds engendró «ese objeto grosero y asqueroso que fue Led Zeppelin») y la iconografía motera de «Born to Be Wild» de Steppenwolf, cuyo verso «heavy metal thunder» dio nombre al género. Algunos críticos estadounidenses defienden a Iron Butterfly, Steppenwolf o Blue Cheer como primera banda de heavy. En 1971 la crítica ya usa el término: Mike Saunders, en Creem, dice que Sir Lord Baltimore domina «todos los trucos del heavy metal».
scenes.family: Raíces: blues rock, psicodelia y hard rock

scenes.name: Segunda invasión británica y MTV
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: En 1982 el new pop deja de ser un sueño de periodistas: «Don't You Want Me», «Tainted Love» y «The Look of Love» anuncian una nueva invasión, y en 1983 la segunda camada (Duran Duran, Culture Club, Wham!, Eurythmics, Thompson Twins) conquista Estados Unidos gracias a MTV, canal ideado por Michael Nesmith que, sin vídeos americanos, dependía de los británicos, más videogénicos y cultivados en el estilo («I want my MTV»). A Flock of Seagulls, Altered Images («Happy Birthday»), Simple Minds («Promised You a Miracle», New Gold Dream), Haircut 100, Kajagoogoo; Bowie se broncea con «Let's Dance». El new pop reexporta música negra (Chic, P-Funk, Quincy Jones) a la América blanca. En el Reino Unido, 1983 se vive en cambio como un año infausto: reelección de Thatcher, «Kill Ugly Pop» en las paredes y la vuelta de la conciencia social.

scenes.name: El diluvio: invasión británica y garage
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: El Mersey-beat lleva a su conclusión la idea de los Beach Boys (ritmo de rock'n'roll y melodía pop): los Beatles, «la segunda gran estafa del rock'n'roll», popularizan lo que surge del underground. Frente a ellos, las tres grandes bandas británicas de 1964: los Rolling Stones (que redefinen al intérprete, el concierto y la canción rock y fijan el eje cantante-chamán y guitarrista carismático), los Kinks (inventores del riff más famoso y del garage, el hard rock y el heavy metal) y los Animals; los Who llevan al límite el himno generacional y la ópera rock, y los Yardbirds establecen la supremacía de la guitarra. En EE UU la invasión británica desata el garage-rock, los proto-punks de cada ciudad (Kingsmen, Sonics, Standells, ? and the Mysterians, Monks).

podcast.title: Recording with Speaker Damage (1964)
podcast.body: While recording a song in 1964, band member Dave Davies employed an unusual technique to achieve distortion by slashing the speaker cone of his small amplifier. This intentional damage, whether by razor blade or screwdriver, produced a distinctive sound but provided limited control over the characteristics of the distortion. "When the band was recording this song in 1964, he slashed the speaker cone of his small amp."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: BBC Censorship of Father Christmas
podcast.body: The BBC was not enthusiastic about playing "Father Christmas" due to its controversial lyrics, which included themes of mugging a Santa Claus and demands for jobs and even a machine gun instead of toys. This reaction led Ray Davies to comment on a perceived double standard, where new wave bands could express such sentiments, but established artists faced scrutiny. "The BBC was not so enthusiastic about playing this song though, no doubt, because of the lyrics."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
For the Record - The 70s

podcast.title: Band Evolution and Creativity
podcast.body: Formed in 1963 as a blues-influenced rock band, The Kinks went through various phases, including a "rock opera phase" in the mid-70s and later repurposed themselves as an "arena rock band" in the late 70s, gaining a new generation of fans for their live performances. Throughout these transformations, the band consistently maintained creativity in its sound and lyrics, primarily written by Ray Davies. "When the band first formed in 1963, they were a blues influenced rock band like many of the bands coming out of the UK at that time. Their first hit was You Really Got Me, released in 1964."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
For the Record - The 70s

podcast.title: British Invasion Influence
podcast.body: The Kinks are cited as one of the British Invasion bands that followed The Beatles, further developing the sound that would lead to Powerpop. They are considered an influence by later Powerpop acts like Big Star. "Through the Beatles came all the rest of the British invasion bands, especially the Kinks and the Who."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Conceptual Film Experimentation
podcast.body: Around the same time The Monkees were gaining popularity, British acts like The Kinks were experimenting with conceptual films designed to promote their songs and albums. This marked an early phase of artists exploring the visual medium beyond simple performance clips. "At about the same time, British acts like the kinks and the hoo were experimenting with conceptual films designed to promote songs and albums."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Future of the Music Video - Part 1

podcast.title: Contractual Troubles (Two Flops)
podcast.body: After releasing two consecutive flop singles ("Long Tall Sally" and "You Still Want Me") on their three-single contract with Pye Records, The Kinks found themselves in a precarious position. It seemed "entirely likely" that the record label would drop them after the release of their next single, making the subsequent success of "You Really Got Me" critical for their survival. "They'd had two flop singles in a row on a three single contract. It seemed entirely likely that the label would drop them after the next single."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 119: "You Really Got Me" by the Kinks

podcast.title: Dave Davies' Guitar Contributions to Father Christmas
podcast.body: Dave Davies, brother of Ray Davies, found "Father Christmas" to be a "very special" song due to the "opportunity to put interesting guitar parts in there," including "guitar riffs that I think sound great." He also appreciated the "little Christmasy chimes and stuff" which he considered part of the "theater of the tune," alongside the song's message about socio-economic disparity during the holiday season. "Dave Davies, brother to Ray, said this of the song. Father Christmas is very special to me because it was an opportunity to put interesting guitar parts in there. Guitar riffs that I think sound great."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
For the Record - The 70s

podcast.title: Early Creativity vs. Label Sabotage
podcast.body: The Kinks were regarded as second only to The Beatles among British groups in 1960s creativity, but their record label was reportedly more interested in "short term chart success than in artist development," which "sabotaged" their potential. "who were always sabotaged by a record label more interested in short term chart success than in artist development."

podcast.title: Early R&B Exploration
podcast.body: The Kinks were among the British bands in the 1960s who ventured into playing R&B, a style that became part of the Mod culture's evolving musical preferences. "Then British bands trying their handed R&B, like the Rolling Stones and the Yard Birds and the Kinks, and especially the Who."

podcast.title: Early Use of "New Wave" Term
podcast.body: The term "New Wave" was initially used in music to refer to the new generation of bands emerging, including The Kinks. This early usage applied to groups that represented a fresh musical movement departing from mainstream consumption. "Se usaba para hacer referencia a la nueva ganación de los Beatles, los Beach Boys, Rolling Stones, los Kings y de todas estas bandas."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Flexible Early Band Names
podcast.body: In their initial stages, the group was known as the Ray Davis Quartet. However, the name was flexible; if Pete Quayfe or Dave Davis secured a booking, they would sometimes be credited as the Pete Quayfe Quartet or the Dave Davis Quartet, reflecting the fluid leadership in securing early gigs. "they became the Ray Davis quartet, though sometimes if Pete or Dave rather than Ray got them the booking, there would be the Pete Quayfe quartet or the Dave Davis quartet."

podcast.title: Following Sgt. Pepper's Lead & 70s Golden Age
podcast.body: The Kinks were among the bands that got into the act of creating concept albums after the release of The Beatles' *Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band*, and were also mentioned as a prominent act during the golden age of the concept album in the 1970s. "That opened the floodgates, the moody blues, the who, Frank Zappa, the kinks, and a bunch of other bands got into the act."

podcast.title: Graham Nash's Stage Act Intervention
podcast.body: Promoter Arthur Howes sent someone to help The Kinks develop a more "showbiz" stage act. However, this effort was halted when Graham Nash of The Hollies intervened, telling the person to "leave the Kinks alone," asserting that the band was "okay as they are" and did not need further grooming. "Graham Nash of the Hollies ordered him to leave the Kinks alone, saying they were okay as they are."

podcast.title: Mod Revival Inspiration
podcast.body: The Kinks were one of Paul Weller's favorite bands, significantly influencing his deep fascination with the original Mods and his subsequent leadership of The Jam's Mod revival. "Leader Paul Weller had always been fascinated by the original mods and his favorite bands became the Kinks in the Who."

podcast.title: Ongoing Sibling Rivalry
podcast.body: The brothers Ray and Dave Davies of The Kinks have maintained a difficult and ongoing relationship for an extended period, characterizing it as a persistent rivalry. "Ray and Dave Davies are the kinks."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Origin of "The Kinks" Name
podcast.body: Larry Page suggested the name "The Kinks" for the group, capitalizing on the "kinky" buzzword of the day, which gained popularity in the wake of the Profumo sex scandal and the associated rumors of BDSM. The name was chosen to generate "plenty of outrage" but remain "just about broadcastable," also considering the "camp demeanor" of Dave Davis and Pete Quayfe. Despite the group members initially disliking the name, they ultimately accepted it. "Page decided that this was too good an opportunity to miss... it would make sense to call the group The Kinks, as a name that would generate plenty of outrage, but was still just about broadcastable."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Persistent Sibling Rivalry
podcast.body: Ray and Dave Davies of The Kinks are noted for their long-standing and intense sibling rivalry, described as a "bad one" that has continued for an extended period. "Ray and Dave Davies of the Kinks, that's a bad one that's been going on forever."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Previous Reigning Champions of Sibling Rivalry
podcast.body: Before Liam and Noel Gallagher, Ray and Dave Davies of The Kinks were considered the benchmark for intense and long-standing sibling rivalries in music. Their continuous feuding was widely known and documented. "Even crazier than what we've seen with Ray and Dave Davies of the Kinks, the previous reigning champions."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Ray Davies' Songwriting Philosophy
podcast.body: Ray Davies, inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 1990, viewed rock music as an important platform for conveying ideas and opinions, especially about "things I can fight for." He noted that while many songwriters create lighthearted Christmas songs, his "Father Christmas" aimed for deeper social commentary with a "dark humor" approach, addressing the disparity between the rich and poor. He expressed approval for "true punks" like the Ramones and Lou Reed for their genuine expression, contrasting them with bands he felt were merely "jumping onto" trends. "He said he sees rock as an opportunity to get ideas and opinions across, but it's just become opinionated."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
For the Record - The 70s

podcast.title: Rolling Stones Clone Perception
podcast.body: During their first major tour, The Kinks were largely dismissed by audiences as being a "clone of the Rolling Stones." This perception arose because, like the Stones, they frequently performed a similar repertoire of R&B standards common among London R&B bands at the time, with the Stones being the most recognized reference point for that musical style. "mostly being dismissed as being a clone of the Rolling Stones, because like the Stones, they were relying on the same set of R&B standards that all the London R&B bands played."

podcast.body: Following their stint as The Ram Rods, the group changed their name again to The Bull Weevils. "shortly after Ray got serious about the Ram Rhyds, who soon changed their name again to the Bull Weevils."

podcast.title: The Ravens (Early Name)
podcast.body: Around the time of their demo recording session, The Bull Weevils adopted yet another name, becoming The Ravens. This name was chosen in homage to a recent film starring Vincent Price, which itself was based on an Edgar Allan Poe poem. "the Bull Weevils changed their name yet again to the Ravens, naming themselves after the recent film, starring Vincent Price, based on the Edgar Allan Pope poem."

podcast.title: Veterans of the First British Invasion

xref.title: Commercial Flop, Critical Success
xref.body: Big Star, with frontman Alex Chilton, aimed to follow in the footsteps of The Beatles and The Kinks while also admiring The Beach Boys' melodies. Despite being major critical darlings with a strong following among other musicians, they struggled with a bad record deal, failed to achieve hit singles, and sold few records, leading to their breakup after three years. "Unfortunately for Big Star, they couldn't manage any hit singles and never sold many records."

xref.title: DIY Amp Modification
xref.body: Dave Davies, frustrated with not getting the right sound from his Vox Elpico amp during a recording session for The Kinks, intentionally hacked up its speaker cone with a razor blade and poked holes in it with a pin. This extreme modification was a deliberate effort to achieve a specific distorted sound. "But not before Brother Dave Davies hacked up the speaker code of his Vox Elpico amp with a razor blade and poking some holes in it with a pin for good measure."
